    DEVELOPMENT OBJECTIVE

    Original Development Objective (Approved as part of Approval Package on 24-Jul-2023)
    The project development objectives of KWSCRP-1 are to: (i) increase availability and productivity of irrigation water for
    project beneficiaries; and
    (ii) enhance the institutional framework and strengthen capacity for water security and climate resilience for thecountry.

    (a) increase access to irrigation water for project beneficiaries and (b) enhance the institutional framework and strengthen
    capacity for water security and climate resilience in certain areas of the territory of the Recipient.

    I.   PROJECT CONTEXT AND DEVELOPMENT OBJECTIVES

A.       CONTEXT AT APPRAISAL

1.      Country context. Kenya emerged from a decade of uneven growth, with a growth rate of 3.9 percent in the 2000s.
Despite challenges such as political instability, drought, and global crises, the economy rebounded in 2010 with a 5.6 percent
growth rate, driven by reforms and infrastructure investments, while it slowed to 4.4 percent in 2011.1 Extreme poverty
affected nearly half of the population, with 80 percent of the poor in rural areas dependent on agriculture, contributing 24
percent to gross domestic product (GDP), 62 percent of formal employment, and 60 percent of exports. Its productivity
hinged on rainfall and water access. Kenya had launched Vision 2030, which was approved by Parliament in 2012, aiming
to become a middle-income country by 2030. This ambitious plan targeted a 10 percent annual GDP growth to transition
from poverty to shared prosperity and focused on three pillars: economic, social, and political. Key to its success was
achieving water security and reducing climate vulnerability for sustained growth, equity, and social stability.2

2.       Water resources context. At the time of the project appraisal, Kenya’s freshwater resources were estimated at
526 m3 per capita annually, and the country was classified as a ‘water-scarce’ country. The water scarcity was predominantly
concentrated in arid and semiarid lands, which account for over 80 percent of the country’s area and were home to 20
percent of the population. Meanwhile, other more populated regions faced challenges related to the limited productive use
of available water resources or exposure to floods. With rising population, economic growth, and urbanization, there was
increasing competition for the use of the limited water resources. In 2012, only 60 percent of the urban and 40 percent of
the rural population had access to safe drinking water, and only 90,000 ha out of a potential irrigated area of 539,000 ha had
been developed. Close to 26 million ha of agricultural land was dependent on unpredictable rainfall. Kenya faced the
additional challenge of high inter- and intra-annual rainfall variability that resulted in frequent droughts and floods. A post-
disaster needs assessment estimated that the overall effects of the 2008–11 drought cost the economy US$12 billion.3

3.       Rationale for World Bank engagement. The Government of Kenya (GoK) had planned a large-scale water
investment program to address water challenges and close the massive investment gap in water sector infrastructure that
had been estimated at US$5–7 billion in various studies. The Water Sector Strategic Plan (2010) of the Ministry of Water,
Sanitation and Irrigation (MoWSI) that focused on reducing the water investment gap found substantial opportunities for
multipurpose storage to secure reliable water supply, manage floods, provide irrigation, and generate hydropower. The
World Bank Kenya Country Partnership Strategy (2010–2013)4 supported the GoK’s Vision 2030 for sustainable growth,
including water security and reducing climate change impacts. The GoK requested the World Bank to support its ambitious
plans in closing the investment gap for the water sector through a long-term and transformational program aimed at building
water security and climate resilience for economic growth. The provisions of Kenya’s Constitution, which was adopted in
2010, included the devolution of certain functions from the national level to 47 counties. This entailed a redefinition and
realignment of roles and responsibilities and the creation of new organizations for the water sector. The urgent need to invest
in priority water infrastructure, while at the same time aiding the GoK to establish the requisite enabling institutional and
legal foundation to improve the performance and sustainability of the water sector, called for a pragmatic approach of phased
support. This project was designed to respond to this need.
4.      Theory of Change (Results Chain). At the time of appraisal, the project’s Theory of Change (ToC) was not
required. Figure 1 has been created for this Implementation Completion and Results Report (ICR) and is based on the 2013
Project Appraisal Document (PAD) information.

3

4
  World Bank. 2010. Kenya - Country partnership strategy for the period FY2010-13. Washington, DC: World Bank.

5.      Project Development Objectives (PDOs). As per the Legal Agreement, the original PDO was to: (i) increase
availability and productivity of irrigation water for project beneficiaries; and (ii) enhance the institutional framework and
strengthen capacity for water security and climate resilience for the country.

B.       SIGNIFICANT CHANGES DURING IMPLEMENTATION

7.       The KWSCRP underwent seven restructurings as follows to address changing challenges and priorities:

     (a) First restructuring (June 2015): Added US$58 million in financing, a US$3.5 million grant from the Korea World
         Bank Partnership Facility Trust Fund, and reallocated US$25 million, expanding the scope to improve water
         services in Mombasa County, strengthen flood infrastructure and early warning systems, and enhance the Nzoia
         watershed.
     (b) Second restructuring (September 2017): Addressed delays in major contracts and low disbursement due to limited
         readiness and procurement inefficiencies that lead to streamlined implementation arrangements, revise the result
         framework (RF) and canceled US $ 13 million.
     (c) Third restructuring (June 2019): Reduced project scope and cancelled uncommitted funds (US $ 70 millions) in
         response to persistent implementation setbacks, especially procurement and land acquisition delays, to focus on
         achievable objectives.
     (d) Fourth restructuring (February 2022): Dropped the PDO indicator, reduced the scope, adjusting RF and reducing
         expectations and targets due to continued land acquisition delays.
     (e) Fifth restructuring (November 2022): This restructuring followed a breakthrough agreement with MoWSI, National
         Irrigation Authority (NIA), and National Land Commission (NLC) that resolved land acquisition bottlenecks and
         enabled LNISP-1 project delivery, leading to a nine-month extension. Based on the principle of minimizing
         involuntary resettlement impact, maintaining the sustainability and ownership principles of the infrastructure
         considering international and in- country experiences, the GoK agreed to: (a) reduce the footprint of the farm canals
         (tertiary canals) through revision of the design; and (b) only construct tertiary and feeder canals where farmers
         voluntarily consented to provide access to the canal construction on a minor portion of their farm in return for
         receiving irrigation water access through this productive asset.
     (f) Sixth restructuring (September 2023): Provided a two-month extension to finalize preparations for additional
         financing.
     (g) Seventh restructuring (October 2023): Secured US$30 million in new financing and extended the closing date by
         18 months to May 2025 to complete LNISP-1 and reinstate its original targets. See more details on annex 7.

8.       Revised PDOs. The PDO was revised during the 2022 restructuring to (a) increase access to irrigation water for
project beneficiaries and (b) enhance the institutional framework and strengthen capacity for water security and climate
resilience in certain areas of the territory of the recipient. The revision involved replacing ‘availability and productivity of
irrigation water’ with ‘access to irrigation water’ for project beneficiaries in part (a) and replacing ‘for the country’ with ‘in
certain areas of the territory of the Recipient’ in part (b).

9.     Revised PDO indicators. During restructurings, PDO indicators were dropped, reworded, added and PDO targets
were adjusted to be more focused on achievable outcome.

     •   The original PDO indicator related to “productivity of irrigation water” was dropped entirely in 2022.
     •   The PDO indicator for irrigated area was revised: its target was reduced from 4,043 ha to 777 ha in 2019, then later
         adjusted to 2,385 ha in 2022, and finally reinstated to 3,904 ha in 2023 as project scope and financing changed.
     •   The original PDO indicator, “Water Policy adopted and Water Bill submitted to Parliament,” was later revised to
         “Water Act, Sector Policy, and Regulations adopted”, similarly, the original indicator as “Satisfactory ratings of



                                              Official Use Only                                                           Page 3
         The World Bank
         Kenya Water Security and Climate Resilience Project (P117635)                                     ICR DOCUMENT


         key water institution performance contracts”, was revised to “Percentage of institutions mandated by Water Act
         established (%)”.
    • Additional PDO indicators were introduced, including “the establishment and operationalization of the Water
         Resources Authority”, and “the number of people with increased flood protection” to reflect enhanced institutional
         framework capacity for water security and climate change.
10.      Revised components. The first component of the project, that is, Water Resources Development, had its scope
expanded under the first restructuring in 2015 to include (a) the construction and rehabilitation of flood protection
infrastructure to protect the irrigation infrastructure and approximately 66,700 people living along the banks of Lower Nzoia
River, (b) Nzoia watershed management activities, (c) upgrading and expansion of the flood forecasting and early warning
system (FFEWS) for Lower Nzoia River basin, and (iv) rehabilitation of priority sections of the water distribution network
in Mombasa to reduce water losses.

Other Changes

11.      Changes to Result Framework (RF): The intermediate result indicators (IRIs) were repeatedly revised during
restructurings to reflect changes in project scope, feasibility, and lessons learned during implementation. It was revised
during five key restructurings: the 2015 restructuring made targeted adjustments to IRIs, including cancelations, additions,
and revisions; the 2017 restructuring adjusted PDO-level indicators and adjusted/canceled IRIs; the changes to the RF in
2019 included reductions to the scope of the indicators and the inclusion of new indicators; the 2022 restructuring involved
the dropping of a PDO indicator, target adjustments, and the addition of new indicators; finally, the 2023 restructuring
corrected the targets and scope of the indicators at project closure. For a detailed summary of modifications to the RF, please
refer to Annex 7, Table 7.2.

12.      Some of these changes to IRIs included dropping and replacing indicators. Several intermediate indicators were
dropped, especially those related to agricultural productivity (e.g., cropping intensity, value of agricultural products
marketed) and Mombasa water utility performance (e.g., non-revenue water reduction, revenue collection efficiency), as
these outcomes became unachievable. Few were replaced or merged. For example, the indicator on “establishment and
operationalization of basin water resources committees (BWRCs)” was replaced by “Water Resources Authority (WRA)
established and operational,”. While New intermediate indicators were introduced such as: “Operational IWUAs created or
strengthened”, “Number of Sub-catchment Management Plans (SCMPs) revised/developed and implemented”, “Six Basin
Plans Developed and Adopted”, “Land area under sustainable land and water management in Nzoia watershed”, and gender-
focused indicators was introduced too, as “female representation in IWUA leadership”.

Rationale for changes and their implication on the original theory of change

13.      The project’s seven restructurings responded to evolving implementation challenges and opportunities (see para. 7
and Annex 7). The main implication for the theory of change was the 2022 removal of productivity-related indicators,
shifting the ToC to emphasize access to irrigation water, institutional strengthening, and pathways to resilience and water
security. The initial ToC figure reflecting this shift was developed during the 2022 restructuring and is presented in Annex
2, Figure 1.

          The World Bank
          Kenya Water Security and Climate Resilience Project (P117635)                                     ICR DOCUMENT


 II.     OUTCOME

A.      RELEVANCE OF PDO

Assessment of Relevance of PDOs and Rating
Rating: High

14.      At closing, the PDOs aligned closely with the World Bank Group’s Kenya CPF (FY2023–2028), which prioritizes
improving water security, increasing household resilience to shocks, and extending infrastructure services to the last mile —
toward outcomes of greater natural capital resilience and more equitable service delivery. KWSCRP investments—LNISP-
1 irrigation infrastructure, flood protection benefiting 66,700 people through dyke construction, expansion of Mombasa’s
drinking water network, and institutional strengthening—directly support these objectives. The project’s legal and
institutional reforms, including operationalizing the Water Resources Authority, training 571 officials, and supporting the
Water Act and sector policy, bolster governance and institutional effectiveness. Collectively, by improving water
management, advancing climate adaptation, and strengthening sector institutions, the PDO advances Kenya’s Vision 2030
and the CPF’s goal of an inclusive, resilient, middle-income economy.
15.     The PDOs remain highly relevant to Kenya’s development priorities. The KWSCRP PDO addressed climate change
vulnerabilities, strengthens institutional effectiveness and water security, and is well aligned with the focus of National
Climate Change Action Plan 2023–2027 and Kenya’s Country Climate and Development Report (2023). LNISP-1
development also complements Kenya’s National Irrigation Sector Investment Plan (NISIP) 2025–2035 and the
Agricultural Sector Transformation Strategy, both of which prioritize irrigation expansion and productivity gains. The PDO
makes significant contributions to Kenya’s Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), notably SDG 2 (zero hunger), SDG 6
(clean water), SDG 13 (climate action), and SDG 5 (gender equality).
16.    Given its strong alignment with national priorities, World Bank strategic documents, and global SDGs, the
Relevance of the PDO is rated High.

B.      ACHIEVEMENT OF PDOs (EFFICACY)

Assessment of Achievement of Each Objective/Outcome

Rating before 2022 restructuring: Substantial
Rating after 2022 Restructuring: Substantial

17.      The project had a PDO change (concurrent with Restructuring 4), two AFs (concurrent with Restructurings 1 and
7), two cancelations (concurrent with Restructurings 2 and 3), and three extensions of the closing date (concurrent with
Restructurings 5, 6, and 7). Therefore, the project efficacy is assessed using the original and revised indicators before and
after Restructuring 4 in February 2022, which removed the irrigation water productivity PDO and its related IRIs as a major
change in project scope and RF. While other restructurings primarily adjusted PDO targets, modified IRIs and extended the
project timeline, thus, for simplicity and directing focus on the project’s turning point, 2022 restructuring was considered
in the split rating.

18.     In each instance, the attainment of the relevant PDO elements and sub-elements, specifically PDO element A1:
Increase availability (later revised to access) of irrigation water; A2: Increase productivity of irrigation water (subsequently
omitted); B1: Enhance institutional framework; and B2: Strengthen capacity for water security and climate resilience, is
evaluated against the corresponding RF indicator targets. The extent of achievement of the original and revised PDOs are
provided in Table 2.

19.      The IRIs for both outcome 1: increase availability and productivity of irrigation water and outcome 2: Enhanced
institutional framework and capacity for water security and climate resilience, relative to original and revised targets are
provided in Annex 7, table 7.3.
20.      The KWSCRP aimed to invest in complementary water infrastructure for climate change adaptation and to
strengthen Kenya’s WSIs. For this purpose and guided by its ToC, the project sought to increase water availability (PDO
A1) through the construction of LNISP-1 to expand irrigated areas and support its operation and maintenance (O&M)
planning. It also aimed to improve water productivity (PDO A2) by supporting agricultural activities and farmer practices
in the LNISP-1 area to better use delivered irrigation water. The project intended to support the ongoing devolution process
in the country and build strong water institutions (PDO B1) by reinforcing institutional frameworks, approving the Water
Act and policies, enabling institutions to fulfill their mandates, building capacity, and developing water management plans.
Additionally, it anticipated enhancing beneficiary resilience (PDO B2) through interventions for water security and climate
adaptation for emerging national needs by improving understanding and physical capacity in this domain. The project also
aimed, through some IRIs, to bridge water and climate information gaps by expanding/upgrading hydrometeorological
stations and address future water and climate resilience investment planning and needs through developing feasibility studies
and master plans.
21.       The original PDO and IRIs were repeatedly modified over seven restructurings, but the project largely maintained
its initial objectives by adjusting targets—except for water productivity, which was removed in 2022. Each PDO indicator
is reviewed individually below.



                                            Official Use Only                                                        Page 6
           The World Bank
           Kenya Water Security and Climate Resilience Project (P117635)                                ICR DOCUMENT


22.      PDO A1: Increase Access to Irrigation Water (Substantial for original targets; High for 2022 restructuring
targets). The PDO originally aimed to complete LNISP-1 construction and its indicator was targeted to track I&D services
to the estimated command area (4,043 Ha), which was more precisely measured later in 2023 to be 3905 Ha. The November
2, 2025 ICR mission reported that the contractor continued work after project closure in May 2025 and made progress. As
of November 2, 2025, LNISP-1 has completed 78 percent of civil works following measures and steps in a post closure
action plan agreed by client and the Bank that enables the likelihood of its completion by the client. As of November 2,
2025, the scheme is providing I&D services to 2,457 ha—60.7 percent of the original estimated target (4,043 ha) or 63
percent of the final measured command area; and full achievement as 103 percent of the revised target (2,385 ha) in 2022—
and benefiting 8,142 farmers, as shown in Table 2. During the 2022 restructuring, access was defined as water being
available within 250 meters of a farmer’s field. The team determined that constructing all tertiary canals within a block
would serve as an effective proxy for measuring water access for all farmers in that block according to the 250-meter
standard, irrespective of the completion status of feeder canals. Additionally, such construction does not necessitate heavy
machinery and can be completed manually by the farmers themselves, while the scheme office is equipped with O&M
equipment through this project and is there to help farmers to a large extent. Without LNISP-1, these 8,142 farmers would
have depended entirely on rain-fed agriculture, leaving their yields highly exposed to rainfall variability as had been the
case for decades in this area. With LNISP-1, farmers can now receive gravity-fed irrigation for next several decades,
provided the scheme is properly operated and maintained.

23.      The LNISP-1 construction primarily advanced towards the end of the project period (2018-2026) due to the need
to revise feasibility studies, face procurement delays, and address protracted land acquisition bottlenecks. The team
navigated initial challenges and dealt with them consistently, prioritizing achievable outcomes throughout implementation.
In response to these evolving circumstances, LNISP-1 targets were strategically revised from the estimated command area
4,043 ha to 777 ha in 2019, then to 2,385 ha in 2022, and finally to the measured command area 3,905 ha in the 2023
restructuring. While the final completion attempt of LNISP-1 introduced through the 2023 restructuring and AF did not
fully complete the scheme (see Key Factors During Implementation section), by November 2, 2025 the project had
completed 78 percent of LNISP-1 civil works and the GoK committed to complete the remaining sections in post closure
action plan. This highlights the likelihood of achieving the full PDO target for A1 in near future. An aerial view of the
scheme can be visualized here5.
24.     Notably, the 78 percent works completed encompass the most complex components such as intakes, the main canal,
80 percent of distributary canals, three spillways, substantial auxiliary systems and most part of main drainage system .
Significant progress has been achieved in the upper hilly Blocks 1–7, where mostly all tertiary and feeder canals have been
constructed. The remaining activities—including the finalization of tertiary canals, land development and less complex parts
of secondary drainage sections in the lower flat Blocks 8–14, require less investment and lighter equipment, leaving simpler
components to be addressed by GoK at a later stage. In addition, 88 percent of the necessary land parcels for infrastructure
have already been aquired, facilitating the efficient and likelihood of completion of pending work.
25.      The progress of LNISP-1 was thoroughly validated by two ICR missions (May 30 and November 2, 2025), which
included comprehensive site visits, structured interviews with key project stakeholders such as PMU and PIU staff,
supervising consultants, contractors, and interactive focus group discussions with farmers. The annual progress of LNISP-
1 was further corroborated through project documentation. For a detailed overview, Annex 7 provides a schematic layout
map (figure 7.1) and a descriptive summary of completed and remaining works at project closure. Moreover, the project
established the Scheme Project Implementation Unit (SPIU) within the National Irrigation Authority (NIA) and created 14
IWUAs covering all scheme blocks, and enhanced thier capacity-building and achieved inclusive leadership measures,
including women's representation in IWUA’s bodies, meeting IRI 1.3 and 1.4 in Table 2. The development of an O&M
manual clarified operational responsibilities between SPIU and IWUAs, defined irrigation fee collection procedures as well,


5
    LNISP-1 aerial view by NIA https://youtu.be/920t_PERQWo?si=O2yRyqam2uvYnpV0


                                              Official Use Only                                                     Page 7
            The World Bank
            Kenya Water Security and Climate Resilience Project (P117635)                                                                   ICR DOCUMENT


and provided necessary O&M equipment such as heavy machinery. These provisions were verified during ICR mission
visits.

26.      Moreover, the project also supported future investments by developing an investment framework and completing
12 preparatory studies for the investment pipeline including preparation of RAPs for LNISP-1. These studies included water
supply master plans for Kwale, Upper Rift Valley, and Tanathi Regions, and four RAPs for LNISP-1, fulfilling IRI 1.5 and
1.6. The project contributed to the preparation and appraisal of the Mwache Dam under KWSCRP-2 and the development
of the National Irrigation Sector Investment Plan (NISIP) for 2025–2035, reinforcing Kenya’s strategic approach to
irrigation development. Annex 7 Table 7.6 provides details on the scope and value of these investments, and the NISIP is
available online for reference6.

27.      PDO A2: Increase Productivity of Irrigation Water (Modest for original targets; dropped at 2022
restructuring). The project was set out to maximize the use of delivered irrigation water through agricultural support
interventions in LNISP-1. Although the final completion of the LNISP-1 scheme was delayed and water productivity
indicators (PDO A2.1 and A2.2, IRI 1.1 and 1.2) were ultimately dropped during the 2022 restructuring, the project's
commitment to improving productivity remained evident. Notably, under the project, KFW partnership ensured continued
agricultural support in the Bunyala scheme within the LNISP-1 command area, where farmers had already relied on pumped
irrigation. Based on advancement of LNISP-1, the Bunyala scheme, originally covering about 238 ha in Block 8, benefited
from gravity-fed LNISP-1 water, eliminating the need for pumps.
28.     Project-supported agricultural interventions expanded the irrigated area in Bunyala to approximately 1,000 ha
across adjacent Blocks 7, 9, 12, and 13, and enabled increased yields from the baseline for major crops —paddy, banana,
passion fruit, maize, and tomato—fulfilling PDO A2.2. While PDO A2.1 (agricultural production per m³ of water) was not
measured after 2022 due to intensive field requirements, the combination of higher yields and double-cropping suggests
improved productivity per unit water. Further details on Bunyala and the A2 indicators, as captured by the ICR survey, are
provided in Annex 7..
29.     While some activities related to water productivity were scaled down in 2019 restructuring, the agriculture
subcomponent support under the project delivered tangible benefits to farmers. It directly benefited 33,400 farmers—
surpassing the target of 31,500 (IRI 1.8)—through extension services, targeted training, and value chain support. Training
in good agricultural practices, value chain development for key crops (rice, kale, and vegetables), irrigation management,
and the System of Rice Intensification (SRI) reached 11,700 of the 12,600 targeted farmers (IRI 1.7). As a result, in Bunyala,
3,000 rice farmers adopted SRI, experiencing a 30 percent increase in yields, the ability to cultivate two seasons per year,
and substantial savings on seed and labor costs.
30.     The project also strengthened farmers’ linkages with the private sector companies, cooperatives, local markets
linkages, to improve access to inputs, mechanization, finance, markets and quality seedlings, ultimately enhancing value of
agriculture products marketed (IRI 1.2). As a result of this support, even farmers without immediate gravity-water access
during construction initiated farmer-led irrigation using buckets and pumps from scheme canals. With improved varieties,
weed and pest management, and better harvesting practices, these farmers increased productivity; where gravity water was
available, farmers shifted from one to two seasons annually. The recent 10-year lease with Nile Logistics Ltd to modernize
and operate the Usonga Siriwo Rice Mill, supported by KWSCRP, processes rice for Bunyala farmers, indicates the
increased rice production in the area and fostered private-sector linkages by project interventions7.
31.      The positive impact of the interventions was confirmed by an ICR M&E survey of 250 farmers—primarily in the
Bunyala scheme and surrounding areas within the LNISP-1 area. Of these respondents, 88% reported increased yields (PDO
A2.2) for major crops—paddy, banana, passion fruit, maize, and tomato—along with two cultivation seasons annually
indicating higher cropping intensity (IRI 1.1) of 170 percent. These outcomes in Bunyala clearly demonstrate high relevance

 Kenya NISIP https://www.irrigation.go.ke/sites/default/files/downloads/NISIP_compiled%20GREEN_19.03.2025%20V19-1.pdf

 Rice Mill upgrade in project year: https://www.citizen.digital/article/siaya-county-signs-10-year-lease-to-upgrade-and-operate-usonga-siriwo-rice-mill-n374098

                                                          Official Use Only                                                                                 Page 8
          The World Bank
          Kenya Water Security and Climate Resilience Project (P117635)                                     ICR DOCUMENT


and lasting benefits for farmers. The transition from pumped to gravity-fed irrigation, together with agricultural support,
underscores the project’s transformative impact and contributes to even greater results with full LNISP-1 completion across
the scheme command area.

32.      PDO B1: Enhance Institutional Framework (the rating remained High both before and after the
restructuring). It aimed to enhance water sector institutions and refine the policy framework, with notable progress
evidenced by the approval of the Water Act and the adoption of associated policies and regulations through project support
(PDO B1.1). Furthermore, the Water Act mandated compliance for all sector institutions (PDO B1.2), including the
establishment of thirteen Water Works Development Agencies (WWDAs) and the Water Resources Authority (WRA) (PDO
B1.3). In 2016, legal reforms were accomplished through the Water Act, ensuring alignment with the 2010 Constitution.
These reforms provided a foundation for devolution within the sector and facilitated institutional development as well as
the establishment of key agencies. The Water Sector Transition Plan (WSTP) was comprehensively prepared and adopted,
and Kenya’s national water policy received Cabinet approval. Organizational reviews for various entities—including WRA,
the Water Services Regulatory Board, the National Water Harvesting and Storage Authority, and the Water Sector Trust
Fund—were completed and ratified by their respective boards, resulting in these agencies being reconstituted in accordance
with the Water Act 2016. Cabinet endorsement and gazettement of criteria for establishing WWDAs led to the creation of
multiple agencies. While cabinet approval contributed to some delays, the enactment of the Water Act and related policies
represented significant milestones in consolidating sectoral policies and institutional mandates, an achievement
corroborated by ICR structured interview with key officials and previous project members.

33.       Moreover, the project built capacity across key institutions—MoWSI, NIA, WRA, and KMD—by training 571
officials and providing essential technical assistance, tools, and systems, thereby meeting IRI 2.3. WRA was established
and strengthened through training, office equipment, and modern decision-support systems, consolidating its regulatory
role. It prepared river basin plans for six major rivers (IRI 2.1), sectoral and national plans, and 59 sub-catchment plans (IRI
2.6), and supported guidelines for groundwater, surface water, and water quality management. KMD’s flood forecasting
role was also enhanced. Table 7.7 in the annex 7 summarizes outcomes of legal and institutional reforms and capacity
building, corroborated by ICR interviews with WRA, NIA, and MoWSI officials. The project modernized Kenya’s FFEWSs
by installing or upgrading 105 hydromet stations nationwide (IRI 2.2 and 2.9), significantly improving data availability for
flood risk management, and provided targeted training, equipping WRA and KMD with FFEWSs. During the ICR mission,
10 hydromet stations were randomly visited, the FFEWS portal was verified, and structured interviews with the FFEWS
team lead and project members confirmed these results.

34.      PDO B2: Strengthening Capacity for Water Security and Climate Resilience (the rating remained High both
before and after the restructuring). The project defined capacity for water security and climate resilience as enhancing
infrastructural and analytical capacity to understand and manage hydrological variability, with the PDO measured by the
number of direct beneficiaries. At closure, the project reached 158,791 direct beneficiaries, surpassing the original target of
20,000 and the 2022 revised target of 148,316. These beneficiaries included 8,142 LNISP-1 irrigation farmers, 66,700
people protected from floods, and 34,320 participants in agricultural activities (extension services, training, and value chain
linkages support). Additionally, 571 staff from WRA and other institutions received specialized training. The Mombasa
water distribution network connected 18,000 people, and 31,058 individuals benefited from watershed management
initiatives, including community spring protection and school rainwater harvesting tanks. The 66,700 people protected from
floods was elevated to a PDO-level indicator (PDO B2.2) in 2017. These interventions enhanced beneficiaries’ capacity to
understand and cope with hydrological variability.

35.     At the end of the project, in an ICR M&E survey of 402 households in Busia and Siaya Counties protected by flood
dykes, 65 percent and 59 percent of respondents reported they experienced floods “very often” and “often,” respectively,
without the project intervention of constructing the dykes. These figures dropped to 0 percent and 10 percent for the similar
question about flood frequency experienced after the dykes were constructed, which confirms the 66,700 population


                                             Official Use Only                                                          Page 9
         The World Bank
         Kenya Water Security and Climate Resilience Project (P117635)                                   ICR DOCUMENT


effectively protected by dykes. Similarly, M&E surveys confirmed that 88 percent of 402 agriculture participants received
services such as training, extension, or input support, validating the figure of 34,320 farmer beneficiaries.

36.     At project closure, all added or modified IRIs during restructurings were substantially achieved. Sustainable land
and watershed management across 1,830 ha in the Nzoia watershed (IRI 2.7 achieved its target of 1,450 ha), led by WRUAs
in five LNISP-1 counties, helped reduce flood risk and sedimentation for LNISP-1. The project connected 3,000
households—about 18,000 people (IRI 2.10)—in Likoni Mombasa county to the water distribution network. During the
ICR mission, the area was visited; 10 households were randomly interviewed; several manholes were inspected; and results
were confirmed through interviews with the PIU, contractor, and 10 beneficiary households.

37.      The project's accomplishments demonstrate the transformative effects of infrastructure investments, institutional
development, and reform, as well as community participation in enhancing water security and climate resilience in Kenya.
In the absence of this project, Kenya would have faced escalating challenges; for instance, approximately 66,700 individuals
would have remained vulnerable to severe flooding, and WSIs would likely have continued to operate in a fragmented
manner without the necessary capacity, coordination, or legal authority to implement major initiatives such as the Mwache
Dam. This scenario would have left the country less equipped to address critical needs in irrigation, water supply, flood
management, and watershed protection. Furthermore, the absence of strategic planning documents, including river basin
plans and NISIP, could have impeded effective water resource management and limited the potential for successful irrigation
development, resulting in suboptimal water sector investment outcomes.

Justification of Overall Efficacy Rating

38.      The overall Project efficacy demonstrated notable progress, being rated Substantial in relation to the original and
the revised 2022 restructuring targets.

39.     For the original project targets: Overall Efficacy was rated Substantial, reflecting full or High achievement of the
second elements of the PDO (B1 and B2). For the first part (A1 and A2), the project reached 60.7 percent (or 63 percent of
the final measured command area) of PDO A1’s targets and completed 78 percent of LNISP-1 complex civil works,
supported by a post-action plan enabling the likelihood of full completion, securing a Substantial rating. PDO A2 was rated
modest, since LNISP-1 scheme only began delivering water to its completed areas by the end of the project, Bunyala and
adjacent areas that received water via the pump system benefited from agricultural interventions and improved major crops
yields (achieved PDO A2.2), while PDO A2.1 was not measured and crop intensity as IRI 1.1 achieved. Moreover, the
project met all IRIs, with shortfalls in investment and pipeline studies (IRI 1.6), and hydromet stations (IRI 2.2).

40.      Under the revised 2022 targets: Overall Efficacy received a Substantial rating, with all PDOs (A1, B1, B2) and IRIs
meeting their objectives. PDO A2 was dropped, only two IRIs remained just short of full completion: flood protection
structures reached 77 percent (IRI 2.8), and the number of people benefiting from the Mombasa water distribution network
stood at 42 percent (IRI 2.10). Importantly, LNISP-1 (PDO A) achieved its targeted outcomes.

C.      EFFICIENCY

Assessment of Efficiency and Rating
Rating: Modest

41.     Economic efficiency. The economic performance of the project is positive. At a social discount rate of 6 percent,
the project yields an economic net present value (ENPV) of US$61.42 million and an economic internal rate of return
(EIRR) of 13.81 percent (over a 30-year period). The economic benefit-cost ratio (BCR) is 3.99. These economic results do
not include the benefits from reduced greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and institutional strengthening at the country level.
The EIRR of 13.81 percent is slightly lower than the ex ante estimate of 14.6 percent at appraisal (2013) but higher than the


                                            Official Use Only                                                       Page 10
          The World Bank
          Kenya Water Security and Climate Resilience Project (P117635)                                       ICR DOCUMENT


revised estimate of 8.9 percent following the project restructuring in 2019. The lower EIRR is primarily due to slow
implementation during the first half, which undermined the project design in terms of ambition, complexity, and cost
estimates. The ENPV of US$61.42 million is significantly higher than the ex ante estimate of US$7.3 million, largely due
to the adoption of a lower social discount rate of 6 percent, compared to 12 percent used at appraisal.

42.      Justification on using updated parameters for economic analysis at project closure. A 30-year analysis period
is used to fully capture the long-term benefits of the project’s infrastructure investments, whose economic life and sustained
benefits extend well beyond two decades. This extended period is also justified by the 13-year implementation timeline, as
most infrastructures became operational in the later years, delaying the accrual of benefits. Thus, a 30-year horizon ensures
the analysis reflects the full operational lifespan of these assets. Additionally, applying a 6 percent social discount rate aligns
with the World Bank’s 2023 Guidelines, which recommend this rate for developing countries to better account for the social
opportunity cost of capital and long-term societal benefits.

43.     To ensure comparability with the appraisal and illustrate the effect of parameter choices,Table 3 summarizes the
key results under different scenarios:

                                      Table 3. Comparison of Economic Analysis Scenarios
                                                          Period       Discount rate
           Economic Analysis Scenarios                                                     EIRR (%)        ENPV (US$, millions)
                                                          (years)           (%)
At appraisal (2013)                                        20              12                14.6                 7.3
At project closure, based on appraisal parameters          20              12                 9.11               −6.3
At project closure, based on updated parameters            30              6                 13.46               57.29
Note: FIRR = Financial internal rate of return.

44.     The financial analysis assessed viability of key project interventions, including flood control, irrigation
development, water distribution network, and catchment protection. The results of the financial analysis, such as internal
rate of return (IRR), net present value (NPV), and BCR, confirm financial viability of these investments for targeted
beneficiaries, particularly in flood-prone and water-scarce areas. Crop yields increased in irrigated zones of LNISP-1 mainly
in Bunyala scheme and adjacent blocks and in areas benefiting from flood protection and enhanced agricultural support.
Annex 4 contains details of the economic and financial analysis.

45.     Design and implementation efficiency. The project’s ambitious design faced substantial early delays due to
complex PMU/PIU arrangements that introduced cumbersome workflows, weakening procurement and financial
management and causing payment delays to contractors and consultants and extended contracts timeline. Project efficiency
was further affected by land acquisition bottlenecks arising from limited readiness for RAP preparation and execution, and
also by LNISP-1 design revisions that took almost four years. The project underwent seven restructurings, including two
cancellations and additional financing to close project financing gaps caused by cost overruns and exchange losses. External
shocks—major floods and COVID-19 restrictions—also disrupted timelines and impeded on-the-ground activities. COVID
was also one factor, at that time land acquisition processes were starting to advance, necessitating land valuations, public
inquires, and public barazas to advance land acquisition, COVID exacerbated these delays. Collectively, these factors
increased administrative and transaction costs (including extended PMU support and international supervision consultant
contracts), raised LNISP-1 contractor standing-time costs and idle-time claims, and at times triggered interest payments due
to delayed disbursements; associated cash-flow constraints and dispute resolution processes further extended contract
durations. As a result the project took 13-year implementation period.

46.     The seven restructuring measures also tackled disbursement issues and improved it particularly in the second half
of the project. By project closure, approximately US$150.12 million had been disbursed, representing a 100 percent



                                               Official Use Only                                                          Page 11
            The World Bank
            Kenya Water Security and Climate Resilience Project (P117635)                                          ICR DOCUMENT


disbursement rate, with 65 percent of the funds disbursed in the second half, reflecting compressed implementation
timelines.

47.        Based on the above discussion, Efficiency of the project is rated Modest.

D.         JUSTIFICATION OF OVERALL OUTCOME RATING

Rating: Moderately Satisfactory

48.      Applying the World Bank’s split rating evaluation methodology for the selected restructuring phases, the project’s
overall outcome is rated Moderately Satisfactory (see Table 4). Feedback from 450 end beneficiaries in ICR M&E surveys,
including water institution staff, consistently reflected satisfaction with the project’s accomplishments. Although initial
challenges stemmed from an ambitious design, limited preparedness, and slower disbursement in the first half, these
obstacles were progressively overcome. The project resulted in a mid-project turnaround that delivered tangible outcomes
relative to ambitious targets across institutions, water sub-sector and regions spread over western and eastern of Kenya
including flood protection infrastructure, Mombasa’s water supply network, 78% completion of LNISP-1 irrigation scheme
with clear completion strategy from GoK, watershed management, FFEWS, and a strengthened investment pipeline.

49.      The project maintained strong alignment with Kenya’s national development priorities and the World Bank CPFs.
By closure, all allocated funds had been effectively disbursed, while over 158,000 direct beneficiaries experienced
strengthened capacity for water security and climate change resilience, supported by advances in water sector reform. The
establishment of the WRA and particularly the adoption of the Water Act, achieved through Cabinet and Parliamentary
approval—stand out as major institutional milestones. The project also strengthened water resources planning, management,
and implementation, laying a foundation for advanced institutions capable of delivering transformative water sector
initiatives such as the Mwache Dam.

50.     Furthermore, the project derived important lessons for a paradigm shift in irrigation development, shifting the focus
toward farmer-led irrigation than large schemes. This direction is now reflected in the design of new Kenya country and
East Africa regional projects, such as Africa RISE (Resilient Irrigation for Sustainable Economy). Overall, despite early
challenges, the project’s achievements have set the stage for high-impact water sector development in Kenya.

E.        OTHER OUTCOMES AND IMPACTS

51.      Gender. A total of around 55,300 women benefited directly from the project (35 percent of the total over 158,000
direct beneficiaries). The project promoted women’s participation through gender sensitization programs, achieving at least
30 percent of IWUA leadership positions for women and a gender-sensitive approach to farmer selection. By supporting
women’s livelihoods and facilitating their involvement in consultations, training, and leadership within WRUAs and
IWUAs, the project empowered women in agricultural, irrigation, and watershed management activities. Women also
benefited from flood management measures—including the rehabilitation and construction of dykes along the Nzoia
River—as women are particularly vulnerable to flood impacts due to social, economic, and legal disadvantages. Community
feedback captured in 402 household M&E surveys highlighted overall high satisfaction among women with interventions
such as the protection of water points and springs for drinking water and domestic use, also from dykes. Moreover, the
project has supported land acquisition in LNISP-1 for women as well, especially widows, by mandating joint compensation
payments, ensuring women’s participation in all consultations, and providing financial literacy training. The project’s GRMs
and committee quotas have helped resolve succession cases fairly, protecting widows’ rights to inherit land and assets.

52.      Poverty reduction and shared prosperity. The KWSCRP has been impactful in advancing poverty reduction and
promoting shared prosperity by supporting water management, agricultural activities, and local economies in Kenya’s most
vulnerable regions. The project provided I&D services to over 2,457 ha, with plans to expand to 3,905 ha that could lift an
estimated 8,000 farmers and their families out of poverty. The project catalyzed local economic growth by creating direct
and indirect jobs during implementation and by enabling improvement of agricultural production, which in turn stimulated
related sectors such as transportation and agro-processing through the market links for high-value crops. The formation and
strengthening of WRUAs empowered disadvantaged groups, especially women, to invest in diverse livelihood options
including beekeeping, livestock rearing, and kitchen gardening, with affirmative action ensuring at least 30 percent female
representation in leadership roles. KWSCRP also prioritized climate resilience and disaster risk reduction, safeguarding
66,700 people through the construction of 34 km of flood protection dykes along the Nzoia River, which improved public
health and enhanced the safety and well-being of communities living in flood-prone areas. Additionally, the project
improved access to water for 18,000 individuals in Mombasa contributing to better health outcomes and quality of life.
Overall, KWSCRP’s integrated approach—combining infrastructure development, institutional strengthening, gender
inclusion, and targeted support for vulnerable groups—has directly benefited over 158,000 people for sustained prosperity.

53.     Institutional strengthening was discussed in the Efficacy section, and mobilizing private sector financing was not
applicable to this project.
