F.      OTHER UNINTENDED OUTCOMES AND IMPACTS

54.      The KWSCRP prepared ground for the second phase of LNISP-2, a future initiative, expected to bring another
4,000 ha under irrigation on the right bank of the Nzoia River. The hydrological feasibility of Phase 2 with detailed design
and bidding documents were prepared, and all supporting structures for delivering water to phase 2 are already constructed
under LNSIP-1, for example, intake gates, size of main canal, spillway, and divert structures. Meanwhile, the northern dykes
already included and constructed the main drainage system for Phase 2’s irrigated lands. Moreover, this project, as
KWSCRP-1 initiated the second project in the program named KWSCRP-2, included the construction of Mwache Dam,
covering its preparation, feasibility study, and appraisal. The Project Implementation Manual (PIM) developed under
KWSCRP-1 is being used for KWSCRP-2, for smooth implementation. Additionally, the empowerment of WRUAs with
developed sub-catchment plans under KWSCRP-1 enabled WRUAs around Mwache Dam to conduct watershed
management activities, essential for controlling sedimentation in the dam. The project also offered significant support to the
National Land Commission (NLC), working closely with its staff to strengthen capacity and assist in implementing its
policies and regulations. By addressing land acquisition challenges, the operation not only resolved issues in LNISP-1 but
also contributed to solving land matters in KWSCRP-2.

 III.    KEY FACTORS AFFECTED IMPLEMENTATION AND OUTCOME

A.      KEY FACTORS DURING PREPARATION

55.      The PDOs were clearly defined, and the RF was largely adequate, capturing the key parameters necessary
to reflect progress toward meeting the PDOs. The design was developed through consultative workshops with
government counterparts and aligned with the World Bank and GoK commitments on climate adaptation, building
institutions and investing in critical infrastructure. A comprehensive and flexible multipronged approach was intentionally
agreed with the client at appraisal to meet emerging needs of the country as water institutions were changing under the
devolution process to strengthen the water sector for economic growth in line with Vision 2030.

56.      Risks and mitigation measures were properly identified at appraisal, and the project was classified as high
risk because of its support to the devolution agenda in the water sector. However early implementation encountered
challenges because some initial mitigation measures, like needing the update of the LNISP-1 feasibility study and the RAP,
proved inadequate. Furthermore the 2010 Constitution shifted water and sanitation services to 47 county governments,
requiring a transition plan, capacity building, and new coordination frameworks. These institutional changes, although
recognized at appraisal, unavoidably created initial implementation difficulties and delays. It’s important to highlight that
the project engaged several agencies, including the MoWSI/PMU and PIUs such as NIA, WRA, MOWASCO, National
Water Harvesting and Storage Authority, NLC, and later the Siaya and Busia County Irrigation Departments, and
interventions spanned Siaya, Busia, Kakamega, Mombasa, and Kwale counties, and hydrometeorological stations were
distributed nationwide.

57.     Moreover, the project’s flexible, pragmatic, and adaptive design principles to respond to Kenya’s evolving
water sector needs also allowed the project to expand its interventions through the 2015 restructuring and AF. This
expansion proved counterproductive and ineffective in a challenging and complex implementation environment. The
scope of the project was broadened to enable the delivery of highly impactful interventions for the country by including
flood infrastructure, Nzoia watershed activities, and support for FFEWS. Additionally, funds were reallocated to introduce
a program aimed at improving water services and management in Mombasa County. However, these expansions presented
implementation burdens and setbacks due to the broad scope and lack of strong implementation measures in place.
Consequently, the restructurings in 2017 aimed to address (a) limited project readiness, (b) complex and inefficient
implementation arrangements, and (c) significant procurement delays. While subsequent restructurings adjusted the targets
and implementation issues and delivered those high impact interventions.


                                            Official Use Only                                                        Page 14
         The World Bank
         Kenya Water Security and Climate Resilience Project (P117635)                                    ICR DOCUMENT


B.      KEY FACTORS DURING IMPLEMENTATION

Factors Subject to the Control of the Government

58.     Delays due to revision of LNISP-1’s poor feasibility study and cost escalation. KWSCRP began in 2013, but
LNISP-1 implementation was delayed until 2018. Between 2013 and 2017, low-quality feasibility study led to revisions,
redesigns, and procurement delays. The revised feasibility study significantly increased the scheme’s estimated cost from
US$37 million to US$58 million, lowering the projected EIRR from 14.6 percent to 9.2 percent. Identifying an appropriate
scheme intake became a complex process with multiple options considered. In 2017, disconnects between procurement and
technical teams further contributed to poor-quality bidding documents.

59.     One significant implementation challenge was the delay stemming from inadequate preparedness in both the
development and application of social and environmental safeguard instruments, especially the RAP. Construction
commencement in 2018 was postponed by around six months because the contractor and project team had not completed
the necessary environmental safeguard compliance documentation due to poor coordination. Even after these issues were
addressed, construction could not begin as land acquisition had not been completed, exposing a critical failure to properly
sequence RAP preparation, clearance, and construction works within the project timeline. This misalignment resulted in
increased costs from contractor standing time, financial setbacks, and ongoing contract disputes, with the contractor even
resorting to renting land to commence works. Land acquisition itself became a major bottleneck, delaying LNISP-1 by over
two years and affecting other interventions such as the Mombasa water distribution network and flood protection structures,
which experienced delays of 7–12 months.

60.      As an example, after two years of LNISP-1 contract commencement, only about 10 percent of the required land had
been fully acquired, largely due to procedural hurdles; reforms and leadership changes at the NLC; ambiguous and
inconsistent land documentation; and capacity gaps within the NLC, PMU, and the World Bank. The land acquisition
process stipulated under the Land Act 2012 is complex and time-consuming, involving multiple steps such as gazettement,
inspection, inquiry, award preparation, and compensation payments, with payment processing alone averaging 3–4 months.
At that stage, these processes had not been fully implemented in the country and there were significant capacity gaps. This,
along with insufficient government funding for compensation, resulted in extended delays.

61.       Farmers’ land and crop compensation communications caused delays. Farmers’ compensation communications
were not timely and clear due to poor stakeholder communication and protracted dispute among beneficiaries. Farmers
initially understood the payment arrangements differently than what eventually unfolded, which led to increased opposition
and additional delays in the project rollout. Typically, when contractors needed temporary access to farmland—for purposes
like land leveling, rehabilitating the Bunyala irrigation block, or acquiring cultivated parcels—there was only a two-month
window to complete the work or complete compensation before the next cropping season began. This short timeframe
complicated construction efforts and raised crop compensation costs if coordination was inadequate.

62.      Project implementation arrangement challenges and payment delays. In the early phase, centralized decision-
making within the PMU with individual consultants and limited empowerment of various PIUs led to unclear roles, weak
coordination, and capacity constraints. Key management tools, including a comprehensive PIM and effective M&E
arrangements, were delayed. Some PIUs including NIA as the main implementing agency for LNISP-1 lacked budget
control, reducing accountability, and with its transition between ministries (Agriculture and Water), coordination became
challenging. Progress across various project components—including institutional framework, LNISP-1, dykes, and pipeline
studies—was hindered by payment delays resulting from complex workflows, multiple approval levels extending to the
National Treasury, parallel funding processes (World Bank Group and KfW), and inadequate contingency planning. These
issues led to cash flow constraints for contractors and, in some instances, resulted in claims and extended project timelines.




                                            Official Use Only                                                        Page 15
         The World Bank
         Kenya Water Security and Climate Resilience Project (P117635)                                   ICR DOCUMENT


63.      Unlocking the Complexities of Project Implementation Arrangements. The project teams held several
discussions to analyze the PMU structure, mapping out reporting arrangements, decision-making processes, and
inefficiencies in approving invoices and deliverables. An action plan was created in 2017 to address the issues identified in
the restructuring paper. This plan included all PIUs in the PMU structure and established component leads and sub-teams
for tasks, with the aim of decentralizing decision-making and streamlining processes to improve efficiency and
accountability. Further, to coordinate these different PIUs, the team conducted a monthly meeting of a Project Steering
Committee (PSC), chaired by the Principal Secretary (PS) with the involvement of the chief executive officers (CEOs) of
the various PIUs. Although PSC was discontinued post COVID-19, PSC monthly meetings improved decision-making as
it properly allocated responsibilities to agencies and strengthen accountability.

64.     The last 18-month extension was not fully utilized, primarily due to the expiration of the LNISP-1
contractor’s contract, delays in obtaining a new contract, and an extended account setup process at NLC. The
Synohydro contract for LNISP-1 ended because uncertainty around additional financing hindered timely action on the
extension. After expiration, poor coordination between the PMU and the World Bank procurement teams delayed processing
of the new contract for several months. Opening an NLC bank account for IDA-funded compensation for project-affected
persons (PAPs) involved prolonged discussions among MoWSI, National Treasury, and NLC. These challenges, along with
two rainy seasons, left less than a year for actual work completion.

Factors Subject to World Bank’s Control

65.     The World Bank collaborated closely with the PMU team and demonstrated responsive management by
successfully implementing seven restructurings over the course of the project. It adjusted the project scope, secured
additional financing, canceled uncommitted funds, and reallocated resources to address readiness and emerging
implementation challenges.

66.      The World Bank maintained a close partnership with the client to identify and resolve challenges
progressively across technical, fiduciary, and safeguards domains. The team conducted regular, hands-on supervision
and provided technical guidance. For example, based on the World Bank’s advice, the project team redesigned part of the
dykes, reducing costs by nearly half as shifting the construction of the dykes to the riverside, minimizing land acquisition
needs. Moreover, the World Bank team also took several measures to strengthen PMU and PIU arrangements for improved
performance, as discussed in the previous section on unlocking project implementation challenges. Fiduciary oversight was
adequate, with the World Bank supporting the PMU and implementing agencies to progressively strengthen FM, address
audit findings, and gradually enhance M&E and procurement processes. Safeguards compliance was monitored, with the
World Bank facilitating RAP implementation and environmental compliance while ensuring grievance mechanisms
remained accessible.

67.      Earlier review of land acquisition requirements and improved coordination during the 2023 restructuring
and provision of additional financing could have mitigated delays in LNISP-1 civil works. Implementing the minimum
impact rule, emphasizing sustainability and local ownership from the outset, and designing more limited land acquisition
areas for LNISP-1 tertiary canals—excluding non-essential access roads—would have likely reduced the duration of delays
related to land acquisition. Additionally, administrative inefficiencies and inadequate coordination between the World Bank
and client procurement teams during the LNISP-1 contract renewal in 2023 resulted in over six months of delays that
ultimately reduced the 18-month extension timeline provided.

Factors outside the Control of the Government

68.    External shocks, including flooding, political instability, and the COVID-19 pandemic, impeded the project's
progress. The 2019 floods, which were the most severe in Kenya since 1961, devastated all rehabilitation works previously
completed in LNISP-1 during the long rainy season from March to June of that year. Consequently, the contractor's


                                            Official Use Only                                                       Page 16
         The World Bank
         Kenya Water Security and Climate Resilience Project (P117635)                                    ICR DOCUMENT


equipment was immobilized for three months, necessitating the re-execution of the works. The turbulent political
atmosphere during the elections of 2013 and 2017, coupled with county-level political interference, delayed decision-
making processes. The pandemic further disrupted supply chains, hampering contractor mobilization and slowing
stakeholder engagement. Social distancing requirements curtailed the frequency and scope of training sessions, community
consultations, and field supervision, while increased costs arose from material shortages and safety measures.

 IV.     BANK PERFORMANCE, COMPLIANCE ISSUES, AND RISK TO DEVELOPMENT OUTCOME

A.      QUALITY OF MONITORING AND EVALUATION (M&E)

Rating: Substantial

69.      M&E Design. A formal ToC was not required at appraisal; however, the relationship between activities, outputs,
outcomes, and the PDO was clear and logical. A comprehensive RF was developed to monitor progress toward outcomes,
with PDO and intermediate indicators disaggregated by gender, location, and sector. The baseline survey provided
sufficiently disaggregated data, and the M&E arrangements for data collection, analysis, and reporting were identified at
appraisal. Some indicators—such as the value of scheme agricultural products per cubic meter of water (a PDO indicator)—
proved difficult to measure and were modified during implementation via project restructurings to improve clarity and
feasibility.

70.     M&E Implementation. Although there were initial delays in forming the M&E team, the project successfully
recruited the necessary staff as implementation progressed, enabling effective monitoring as activities commenced on the
ground. In the absence of a centralized Management Information System (MIS), efforts to develop tailored MIS tools
encountered operational difficulties; consequently, the team used structured Excel workbooks to track tasks and manage
data. These tools supported regular weekly, biweekly, quarterly, semiannual, and annual reporting. Modifications to certain
indicators prompted adaptive improvements to the RF—including refining, redefining, adjusting, or replacing indicators—
to enhance clarity and measurability in line with project objectives. Through these impactful approaches, the project
consistently collected data with clear methodologies, documented and reported progress, facilitating informed decision-
making for all restructurings and adjustments in M&E data management.

71.       M&E utilization. Aligning an effective M&E system for a large, multi-component project proved challenging at
initial stage in the absence of a centralized MIS and a strong M&E team. This contributed to data-quality concerns in early
phases—such as insufficient supporting evidence and inconsistent understanding of results indicators across components in
early stages. The project progressively addressed staffing issues going forward, while regular project meetings helped
surface and address these issues, strengthening data collection, validation and gradually harmonizing methodologies for RF
data collection, analysis, and reporting. As the system matured, M&E findings increasingly supported key decisions,
including project cancellations, additional financing, fund reallocations during restructurings, and modifications to project
scope and sequencing. For example, the M&E data were timely informing both engineering and social teams on land
acquisition priorities and efforts. While opportunities remained for more consistent and comprehensive data collection at
entry and earlier standardization of methods, the M&E system evolved to provide meaningful support for achieving results
and prioritizing activities.

72.      Justification of overall rating of quality of M&E. The overall quality of M&E is rated Substantial. The project
started with a sound RF and baseline design, and, despite early staffing gaps and the lack of a centralized MIS, it instituted
disciplined data tracking and routine reporting that ensured continuity of monitoring. Indicator definitions and measurement
approaches were refined throughout project lifetime to address feasibility and attribution challenges, improving the
robustness of tracking against the PDO. Critically, M&E products were increasingly used to inform high-stakes management
decisions—cancellations, reallocations, additional financing, and scope adjustments—demonstrating the system’s
operational value beyond compliance. While residual limitations persisted, they did not materially undermine the reliability

                                            Official Use Only                                                        Page 17
          The World Bank
          Kenya Water Security and Climate Resilience Project (P117635)                                     ICR DOCUMENT


of results reporting in later phases nor the effectiveness of M&E in guiding implementation across a complex, multi-
component operation. Taken together, design adequacy, adaptive strengthening during implementation, and demonstrated
utilization justify a Substantial rating.

B.      ENVIRONMENTAL, SOCIAL, AND FIDUCIARY COMPLIANCE

73.      Environmental safeguards. The environmental policies that were triggered in this project included Environmental
and Social Impact Assessments (ESIAs); Environmental and Social Management Plans (ESMPs); contractors’ ESMPs;
licensing of ESIAs by the National Environmental Management Agency; Integrated Pest Management Plans; and
Environment, Health, and Safety Plans. These safeguard policies were prepared and cleared by the World Bank, and the
project successfully adhered to them. These instruments were prepared to manage potential adverse impacts on the
environment, construction workers and community health and safety and well-being, community resettlements, and physical
cultural resources from proposed project investments such as the construction of LNISP-1, flood infrastructure, and the
Mombasa water distribution network. The instruments identified the impacts and provided mitigation measures, which were
fully implemented. During the project's implementation, the capacity for managing environment risks within the project by
the implementing agencies was progressively built and enhanced. The PMU, supported by the implementation support
consultants (ISCs) and environmental and social experts, monitored compliance through frequent inspections and monthly
audits. Regular monitoring confirmed improvements in environmental and social risk management. Unfortunately, during
the implementation period, the project sustained two fatalities related to drowning hazard. All construction work was
immediately suspended, investigation was conducted to understand the root causes, and the required corrective actions were
implemented. At the time of project closure, all the Environment and Social Incidents Response Toolkit (ESIRT) cases had
been satisfactorily closed, and the environmental performance rating was ‘Satisfactory’ at end of project.

74.     Social safeguards. The project complied with the World Bank-triggered social safeguard policies including
Operational Policy (OP) 4.12 and OP 4.01. RAPs and the ESMPs were prepared by the client and cleared by the World
Bank. These policies and the accompanying instruments were activated because of potential adverse impacts on land,
structures, and physical cultural resources from activities such as construction of LNISP-1, flood infrastructure, and the
Mombasa water distribution network. In all, four RAPs were prepared and implemented. The processes for developing and
seeking clearance for the RAPs, compensation disbursements took considerable time to finalize; and thus, flagged in project
documents as contributing to overall project slowdowns.

75.       At project closure, of the 4,704 PAPs, 88 percent were compensated, while the remaining were 568 PAPs (12
percent) with a value of around US$883,000. This is mainly due to unresolved issues such as absentee PAPs, succession
grants, pending affidavits, and missing title documentation. Despite substantial efforts during implementation to convert
these cases to ‘payable’, they remained on the non-payable list at project closure, and the borrower retains liability for these
compensations as safeguard policy compliance continues beyond project completion. To address this, the NLC is required
to secure and ringfence the funds until the non-payable PAPs become eligible, with regular reporting and bank statement
verification included in the post-closure safeguard action plan. The World Bank will monitor the implementation of this
plan biannually, including through an ongoing operation of KWSCRP-2 with MoWSI. Throughout implementation, the
ratings for Social Safeguards mostly remained ‘Moderately Satisfactory’ including at project closure.

76.      Grievance redress. A GRM was set up as per the requirements indicated in the ESMP and was functional during
project implementation. Contractors, consultants, and the SPIU had different GRM mechanisms, which were consolidated
with the help of the World Bank team. A total of 156 grievances were reported including compensation, social and
environmental safeguard issues, as well as complaints related to construction and access challenges (that is, need for foot
bridges across canal/drainage channels). The GRM system resolved 142 grievances cases, and efforts are ongoing to address
the remaining 14 which will also be monitored by the Bank biannually including via the ongoing KWSCRP-2 until the cases
are resolved. Out of these 14 cases, 11 pertain to pending compensation matters and are included within the 568 PAPs
awaiting compensation. The remaining three cases concern construction-related issues and beneficiaries’ access inquiries.

                                             Official Use Only                                                         Page 18
         The World Bank
         Kenya Water Security and Climate Resilience Project (P117635)                                   ICR DOCUMENT


77.       Financial management. The project submitted audited financial statements and interim financial reports as
required, meeting the standards for quality and timeliness. The project also maintained a dedicated accountant throughout
the life of the project. The PMU coordinated with the World Bank and relevant PIUs on budgeting and planning, fund flows,
reporting, and auditing. Some of the FM issues faced by the project included delays in the budgeting process due to lengthy
approval processes which led to delays in movement of funds from the Designated Accounts to the project account.
Furthermore, during the initial years of implementation, insufficient funding for the GoK’s counterpart contribution resulted
in ineligible payments—such as interest on delayed payments—being made from IDA funds. These expenses were
subsequently refunded, with substitute documentation provided only at the conclusion of the project. The project was
restructured to incorporate land compensation, which necessitated additional mitigation measures to secure IDA funds. This
included opening a special-purpose account for land compensation using IDA funds, separate from the Government’s pooled
land compensation account. In the 2017 MTR, FM was focused as an area which required substantial strengthening in terms
of fund flow, and timely payment and continuous capacity building undertaken throughout the life of the project.

78.      Procurement. The project faced initial delays due to capacity limitations requiring the provision of training in
procurement and contract management across all levels of PMU/PIUs. Gaps in technical capacities, funds flow between
KWSCRP-1 and KWSCRP-2, multiple financing partners, and the complexity of the initial implementation arrangements
slowed implementation over the project period. This was further compounded by delayed handover of sections of the project
sites for irrigation to the contractor due to land compensation and related environmental and social challenges, changes in
the applicable procurement regulations for AF, and weak procurement and contract management capacity. Lack of effective
planning and synergy between the project teams on site affected the implementation of the environmental and social
component of the project, resulting in lengthy delays and contractual claims, leading to project time and cost overruns. To
mitigate implementation delays, the implementation and institutional arrangements were reviewed and strengthened by
addressing procurement and contract award decision-making bottlenecks, reorganizing procurement workflow, and
enhancing procurement and contract management capacity within the PMU. The World Bank’s procurement team further
provided hands-on procurement and contract management support, expedited reviews and no-objections, and organized
procurement clinics to address capacity gaps, resulting in accelerated disbursement post 2019, while facing procurement
delays in 2023 as well.

C.      BANK PERFORMANCE

Rating: Moderately Unsatisfactory

79.      Quality at entry. The World Bank team designed the KWSCRP with a clear and smart development approach by
focusing on building physical resilience through critical infrastructure investments and strengthening institutions aligned
with Kenya’s 2010 Constitution and Vision 2030 for resilience and economic growth. The project was grounded in analytics;
baselines surveys; sector assessments; and risk, safeguard, financial, and economic analyses. Substantial engagement with
government counterparts ensured technical soundness, the project ambition level, and ownership. For better design, the team
also leveraged lessons from ongoing World Bank operations, such as the Water and Sanitation Service Improvement Project
and the Nile Basin Initiative, which helped address the country’s most critical water needs. Moreover, the project was
closely linked with partner programs and built partnerships to tap co‑financing opportunities; thereby, co‑financing with
KfW for LNISP‑1 was agreed and signed at the initial stage.

80.     Early implementation of the project faced some challenges, mainly due to the complexities of the devolution process
and the need for greater readiness as a high-risk project, discussed in detail under ‘Key Factors During Preparation and
Implementation’ and ‘M&E Design’. Lack of effective project implementation arrangements affected procurement and FM
early on, while the timely preparation and execution of RAPs proved challenging at the beginning, especially as NLC
regulations continued to evolve. Enhanced irrigation expertise within the task team was needed at the initial stage to
proactively address the feasibility study and RAP issues for LNISP-1. As a result, disbursements reached about 8 percent
by the end of the first four years.

                                            Official Use Only                                                       Page 19
         The World Bank
         Kenya Water Security and Climate Resilience Project (P117635)                                    ICR DOCUMENT


81.      Quality of supervision. The World Bank maintained a regular management approach throughout project
implementation. Implementation support missions, ISRs, MTR, and AMs were timely and responsive to emerging issues.
Missions’ AMs, Management Letters, and ISRs candidly highlighted problems and addressed them while keeping the
Country Management Unit and the client informed. ISR ratings accurately reflected project progress and challenges. The
World Bank teams’ collaborative approach, working closely with the client, led to seven project restructurings to manage
the scope of work, realign funds, and address emerging challenges, as detailed in the ‘Factors Affected Project
Implementation’ section. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the World Bank approved adaptive adjustments to workplans,
facilitated virtual supervision, and maintained fiduciary oversight.

82.      The World Bank team also established a good relationship with client counterparts and provided technical guidance
to help advance GoK processes when delays occurred. For example, to address the main bottleneck of land acquisition for
LNISP-1, the World Bank team, together with the client, implemented several impactful measures as outlined below:

        (a)   Hired a resettlement implementation consultant to dissect the process, mapping out the complexity of
              the task and each step and the time required to transition from one phase to another. The role of the consultant
              included guiding PAPs through the process of land acquisition, and assisting them in dispute resolution.
        (b) Improved stakeholder engagement on the ground, to accelerate the land acquisition processes. The
            project team organized regular workshops, bringing together all involved teams, for example, finance, NLC,
            social, PMU, PIU, and PAPs, to foster collaboration and expedite compensation payments.
        (c)   Engaged a legal team. PAPs faced numerous challenges, including succession issues; land jurisdiction
              disputes; and unregistered parcels due to lack of affidavit, title, or green card, which hindered the process. A
              legal team was engaged to address these issues in court, significantly speeding up the resolution.
        (d) Instituted weekly and biweekly meetings focused on land issues and maintained regular dialogues
            among land acquisition team at PMU, NLC, supervising consultants, contractor, surveyor, NIA, and
            succession legal team. These meetings had actionable points for high-ranking officials from NLC, MoWSI,
            and NIA to unlock any encountered matter and were fundamental to ensure coordination between contractor’s
            program and land acquisition prioritization.
        (e)   Unlocked IDA resources for land acquisition. To overcome financial constraints, the team applied for AF
              in 2023 and secured a waiver to allocate IDA resources for land acquisition as a special authorization from the
              Regional Vice President was granted.
        (f)   Revised RAP 4 as specified under paragraph 7 (e).
83.     Therefore, at project closure, NLC CEO expressed “we learned land acquisition through KWSCRP in
Kenya, particularly via LNISP-1, which also supported NLC in acquiring land for other large and complex projects
including Mwacha Dam.”

84.      The World Bank’s implementation performance was also consistently challenged by Kenya’s turbulent context, the
ongoing devolution, the project’s inadequate readiness measures, and emerging implementation issues. Tackling and
unlocking these challenges nearly doubled the original project timeline and left LNISP-1 close to completion at project end.
Despite these compound challenges that affected implementation, particularly in the first half, persistent efforts by both the
World Bank and client teams enabled a turnaround in the second half, with the project adapting to changing PMU and PIU
arrangements and coordination, gradually navigating evolving NLC procedures and social complexities for RAP execution,
strengthening LNISP-1 feasibility study, and mobilizing expertise for irrigation. and continuity was maintained despite high
staff turnover, including six Task Team Leaders (TTLs) over 13 years. Therefore, the Bank team resolved almost all the
issues by closing, the project ultimately took longer. These challenges are discussed in detail in the sections ‘Key Factors
During Implementation’, Quality of M&E’, and ‘Environmental, Social, and Fiduciary Compliance’.



                                            Official Use Only                                                        Page 20
          The World Bank
          Kenya Water Security and Climate Resilience Project (P117635)                                     ICR DOCUMENT


 85.      Despite these challenges, the World Bank team delivered this ambitious 13-year project, achieving substantial
 development objectives and completing 100 percent disbursement in Kenya’s challenging environment. The team delivered
 infrastructure development objectives across regions, institutions, and subsectors and achieved significant institutional
 strengthening and legislative reforms addressing devolution changes. Notably, the establishment of the WRA and the
 adoption of the Water Act are outcomes which required Cabinet and Parliamentary approval and represent substantial
 institutional milestones. The teams’ efforts under the project also prepared institutions to implement more ambitious project s
 and unlocked complexities in land acquisition and irrigation development in Kenya, benefiting ongoing operations such as
 the Mwache Dam and the upcoming operation, the Kenya NISIP support project, under preparation.

86.       Justification of overall rating of Bank performance. Despite adaptive supervision—timely missions and ISRs,
 candid management letters, close client engagement, and seven restructurings the Bank’s performance is rated Moderately
 Unsatisfactory due to material shortcomings that constrained mainly efficiency and few achievements. Quality at entry was
 weak for a complex, multi-component operation in a devolving context: RAP and land acquisition readiness (including
 financing) and implementation/coordination arrangements were underdeveloped; risks related to NLC procedures and social
 complexities were underestimated; and timelines and sequencing were overly optimistic. The project period nearly doubled
 and LNISP-1 remained near completion at closing. While intensive later support enabled full disbursement and important
 project outcome achievements particularly institutional results, while the impact of early deficiencies justifies a Moderately
 Unsatisfactory rating.

 D.      RISK TO DEVELOPMENT OUTCOME

 87.      Financial sustainability risks are associated with the WRA’s responsibility for the O&M of all 105
 established/upgraded hydrometeorological stations and FFEWS under this project. The WRA faces substantial challenges
 due to low user fee collection through water permits and unreliable GoK funding, which affects its ability to maintain the
 stations. Consequently, 89 (85 percent) of the stations were found to be dysfunctional during the ICR mission. As a result,
 data from these stations are not being transferred to FFEWS, preventing the production of early warning systems for targeted
 communities, and the stations and FFEWS have remained non-operational just two years after their completion. New
 regulations have been submitted to the Cabinet to increase water permit fees and enhance WRA's self-sufficiency; these
 need to be approved and implemented as soon as possible to make the stations and FFEWS operational.

 88.     LNISP-1 is well positioned to deliver lasting benefits, while fiscal constraints may delay the completion of the
 scheme, the government has committed to complete the LNISP-1 and operate it safely. These commitments are outlined in
 post closure action plans as (a) the scheme completion strategy endorsed by National Treasury via correspondence dated
 August 28, 2025, (b) an excess water management plan to ensure safety until full scheme completion, and (c) an endorsed
 post-closure safeguards plan. With 78 percent of civil works already accomplished, the ongoing completion of secondary
 drainage systems and the remaining tertiary canals facilitate water flow to lower Blocks (11–14) and ensure safe
 management of excess water during rainfall.

 89.      Sustainability and effective operation of LNISP-1 were supported by the project. NIA has received a detailed O&M
 Manual covering irrigation service fees, maintenance plans, and staffing requirements which has strengthened NIA-SPIU’s
 capacity. The deployment of O&M equipment and the development of a service-oriented water distribution model provided
 effective scheme management measures. Drawing on Kenya’s experience, ongoing capacity building for the scheme
 management unit and securing reliable, predictable O&M financing through user fee collection and/or public funding remain
 necessary. These steps will enhance LNISP-1’s long-term functionality, and service-based irrigation water delivery will
 foster farmers’ accountability. The government also aims to mitigate sustainability risks through NISIP, which places strong
 emphasis on improving O&M performance in existing GoK’s irrigation schemes.




                                              Official Use Only                                                        Page 21
          The World Bank
          Kenya Water Security and Climate Resilience Project (P117635)                                       ICR DOCUMENT


 V.      LESSONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

90.      The KWSCRP became ambitious by adopting flexible and long-term programmatic approach, integrating
institutional and policy reforms with infrastructure development across various water subsectors, regions, and institutions
including major investments for a large scheme such as LNISP-1. In retrospect, implementing large-scale irrigation projects
like LNISP-1 as a stand-alone initiative may offer advantages, as embedding them within broader Investment Project
Financing (IPF) operations like the KWSCRP that combine infrastructure and policy reforms can dilute focus. Furthermore,
institutional and legislative reforms that require Cabinet or Parliamentary approval are often more effectively pursued
through Development Policy Financing instruments rather than being incorporated into IPF projects. These lessons highlight
the importance of carefully considering the appropriate financing and implementation modalities when designing future
water sector programs.

91.     Land acquisition is a critical and often complex aspect of irrigation projects, requiring early planning, legal
preparedness, stakeholder coordination, and adaptive strategies to minimize delays and ensure timely implementation. First,
for LNISP-1, misalignment between construction and land acquisition activities led to delays in site handover, increased
costs due to contractor standing time, and tensions from demands for work acceleration. Therefore, proactive coordination
between land and engineering teams facilitates the identification and prioritization of access areas. Second, farmer
compensation communications must be timely, consistent, and clear. Initially, it was unclear which farmers were affected
or how they would be compensated, leading to misunderstandings and delays. Third, crop compensation must be identified,
coordinated with construction timelines, and appropriately funded. The lack of specific funding for crop compensation led
to construction delays. Future projects should prioritize land acquisition from the outset, strengthen institutional and legal
capacity, secure financing early, and maintain continuous coordination.

92.      LNISP-1 unpacked a lot of lessons in future irrigation development in Kenya, embedded in NISIP as a strategic
document for Kenyan Irrigation development (2025–2035). Its lessons learned placed a hold on prioritizing development
of large-scale irrigation schemes in Kenya. From design to 75 percent completion, LNISP-1 took 13 years, to bring only
2,457 ha of land under irrigation. As a result, NISIP shifted the focus for irrigation development to farmer-led irrigation
instead of large-scale irrigation, based on considerations of implementation speed, impact, and scale to achieve desirable
targeted acreage under irrigation. For large-scale irrigation development in Kenya, or any other large-scale infrastructure
regardless of the sector, drawing on lessons from LNISP-1, a two-stage approach is recommended to ensure strong project
readiness and focused implementation to maximize impact. Stage 1 focuses on feasibility studies, detailed design, and land
acquisition, while Stage 2 involves construction and activities to ensure the sustainability of the outcome (that is, agricultural
productivity, O&M arrangements, and so on).

93.      Technical interventions must be matched by financial planning to safeguard investments and project outcomes.
WRA struggled to maintain 105 hydrometeorological stations and FFEWS due to unreliable funding and low water user fee
collection, resulting in 85 percent of stations and FFEWS becoming nonfunctional within two years. Similarly, LNISP-1
poses sustainability risks. Therefore, a strong focus should be given to O&M of infrastructure during the implementation
period to plan secure and predictable sources of funding, whether through irrigation service fees or reliable government
transfers. Meanwhile, when farmers contribute to the cost-of-service delivery, it fosters accountability and ownership. Well-
designed irrigation water pricing structures balance affordability and financial sustainability. It can also strengthen the
customer–service provider relationship; encourage demand for better services; and, over time, improve system performance.
For future projects, it is essential to develop clear financial strategies including identifying funding sources, assessing
revenue potential, and securing timely regulatory support to ensure systems remain operational and deliver long-term
benefits.
